memories.text: {daughter} is eight, in third standard. Draws on every wall she is allowed to and some she is not, is learning to skate, and has asked for a dog every birthday since she was four.

At {daughter}'s school annual day she danced as a peacock in a costume that took three evenings to stitch. {name} filmed the whole thing beaming with pride and has watched the video maybe fifty times.
{daughter}'s favourite bedtime story is the one about the monkey and the crocodile, told with all the voices. She corrects {name} if a single word changes.

{Their} wife, Shilpa, teaches at a primary school in Vijayanagar. Organised, sharp, the one who remembers every bill and every relative's birthday. She laughs at {name}'s jokes even when they are bad.

{Their} husband, Ravi, is an officer at a cooperative bank. Calm, careful with money, the one who remembers every bill and every relative's birthday. He laughs at {name}'s jokes even when they are bad.
Met {their} spouse at a cousin's wedding in Hassan eleven years ago. 'Love-cum-arranged': they talked for six months on the phone before telling the families, who pretended to be surprised.
{Their} mother, Gowramma, still lives in {hometown} in the old house, keeps two cows and a vegetable patch, and sends a sack of ragi and a tin of homemade pickle with anyone travelling to Bengaluru.
Younger brother Manju runs a mobile phone repair shop in {hometown} and lives with their mother. He fixes everyone's phone for free and is always broke because of it.
{Their} father was a KSRTC bus conductor. In the summer holidays he took {name} along on his route, and {they} learned to call out every stop between {hometown} and the next town.
Grew up at the edge of {hometown}: swimming in the canal after school, stealing raw mangoes from the temple trust's grove, cricket with a plank for a bat until it got too dark to see.
Was the class clown at school, average in marks, best in the class at talking. A teacher once wrote 'can sell sand in a desert' on the report card, and {name} still quotes it.
Did a B.Com at the government college in {hometown}. Hated accounts, loved the college fest, and ran the stall that made the most money three years in a row.
Played kabaddi for the college team, a raider. Now watches Pro Kabaddi on TV with {daughter}, who supports Bengaluru Bulls because {name} does.
Joined the two-wheeler showroom at 23 as a sales executive. Became manager at 30. Mr Shetty, the owner, is old-school: chalk on a blackboard for targets, a coconut broken for every new model.

Runs a team of six salespeople at the showroom: walk-in customers, test rides, finance papers, delivery days with garlands and photographs. Knows the mileage, colours and waiting period of every model by heart.
Proudest work moment: sixty-four bikes in one Navratri season, a showroom record. Mr Shetty framed the sales sheet and it still hangs behind the counter.
Favourite customer story: a farmer who paid for a scooter in coins and notes from three steel tins, counted on the showroom floor for an hour while the whole staff watched.
Rides a black Royal Enfield Classic bought second-hand after the first promotion, washed every Sunday whether it needs it or not.
Rents a two-bedroom flat in Vijayanagar, third floor, with a balcony where {daughter} keeps her plants: two tulsi, one money plant, one chilli that never gives chillies.

Loves ragi mudde with naati koli saaru from {their} mother's kitchen. In Bengaluru the Sunday treat is donne biryani from the place near the bus stand. Makes one dish well, egg curry, and makes it loudly.

Sankranti means going home to {hometown}: the cows decorated, {daughter} handing out ellu-bella to the neighbours. For Ganesha Chaturthi the whole building puts up one big idol and {name} runs the collection.
Sings old Kannada film songs, Rajkumar and S.P. Balasubrahmanyam, at every family function whether asked or not. Puneeth Rajkumar films are the family's Sunday ritual.
Oldest friends are Santosh, now a lineman at the electricity board, and Girish, who teaches at {their} old school. They have known each other since the canal-swimming days.
Has promised {daughter} a family trip to Ooty for three years running; she has already planned the toy train and the boat ride on a sheet of paper stuck on the fridge.
Wants a showroom of {their} own one day, maybe back in {hometown}, and to send {daughter} to a good school that teaches her to swim properly, not in a canal.
Goes to the Chamundi hills temple once a year with the family. Not much of a prayer person, but always buys the bangles and balloons {daughter} wants on the way down.
Kannada at home, a mix of Kannada, Hindi and English at the showroom: whatever language closes the sale.
The joker of every family gathering: nicknames for every relative, impressions of Mr Shetty, a WhatsApp forward for every occasion. {Their} spouse says {they} could make a funeral laugh.
{daughter}'s birthday is in July and is planned months ahead. {name}'s own birthday usually gets remembered by Mr Shetty before anyone at home.
Watches RCB matches at full volume. {daughter} has learned every player's name to be allowed to stay up for the last over.
The phone is never quiet: customer calls, finance agents, the showroom group. {daughter} has set the wallpaper to a photo of herself in the peacock costume and will not let it be changed.
